In Jackson Hole, Warsh Says Fed Policy Isn't Restrictive, Pledges To Tame Inflation

article.title: Warsh's Jackson Hole Debut Signals No Rate Relief as Fed Chair Calls Policy Non-Restrictive
article.excerpt: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh used his first major Jackson Hole speech to argue that broad financial conditions are not restrictive, reaffirm his inflation-fighting focus, and criticize the Fed's forward guidance regime.
article.body_html:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivered a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday that left room for future interest rate hikes and offered little comfort to borrowers hoping for near-term relief. In his first major address at the top of the central bank, Warsh said credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint, directly undercutting the view that the Fed has already tightened enough to bring inflation back to its 2% target.

"Credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint," Warsh told the audience. "Certain sectors like housing and agriculture are showing strains, but on balance, I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive." The remarks solidified his position as an inflation hawk and represented the clearest signal yet that the central bank is not inching toward rate relief.

Warsh acknowledged that the Fed has done a good job on the employment side of its dual mandate, describing labor markets as "broadly consistent with full employment." The U.S. lost 23,000 jobs in July, well off economists' forecasts of roughly 83,000 new jobs, but the unemployment rate ticked down slightly to 4.1%. Still, he said the central bank's predominant focus should now be on prices. "Inflation is running above our 2% target, so the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices," he said.

Beyond the inflation outlook, Warsh used the speech to argue against the forward guidance that has been part of Fed communications since the Global Financial Crisis. He said the central bank should be quieter and more purposeful in its communications, warning that a regime in which investors look primarily to the Fed for their next trade risks blinding policymakers to new developments. "We should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade," Warsh said.

Warsh also framed the economy as being at a "hinge point in history" as artificial intelligence redefines traditional paths to economic growth. He raised open questions about whether AI adoption will produce a sustained productivity boost, how competition among leading models will evolve, and where capital will settle across chipmakers, energy producers, cloud infrastructure providers, and other parts of the AI supply chain. He noted that businesses are rapidly increasing capital expenditures while profit margins remain at historical highs and credit spreads on corporate bond issuance remain strong.

The speech drew from a single full-text account of the event, and the dossier does not include market reaction data, specific policy rate projections, or additional corroborating coverage. What is clear from the available evidence is that Warsh's Jackson Hole debut reinforced a restrictive-leaning posture and signaled that the Fed under his leadership is not preparing to ease financial conditions while inflation remains above target.

drafts.title: Warsh furthers his push toward a ‘quieter Fed’

article.title: Warsh furthers his push toward a ‘quieter Fed’
article.excerpt: In his first Jackson Hole address, new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh doubled down on a promise to cut “forward guidance” and a commitment to 2% inflation.
article.body_html:
At the 100-day mark of Kevin Warsh’s tenure as Federal Reserve chair, the central bank’s message is becoming clearer by saying less. In his first Jackson Hole address, Warsh reinforced a defining theme of his early leadership: the Fed should talk less about what it predicts and focus more on bringing inflation down.

“You can call it an outline. You can call it a trail map. Just don't call it forward guidance,” Warsh said Friday of his own remarks. That line extended a position he has held since his first month in office. At his first Federal Open Market Committee meeting as chair in June, Warsh oversaw the removal of wording in a previous policy statement that may have suggested the Fed anticipated trimming borrowing costs in the future.

Warsh argued that the practice of forward guidance, which the Fed began pushing during the 2007-08 financial crisis, has “overstayed its welcome.” He warned that when markets lean heavily on Fed guidance and the Fed leans on market prices, policymakers risk being “blinded to new developments” and “caught unprepared for a turn of events.” A “quieter Fed,” he said, “is better able to meet its objectives.”

The chair framed the shift as a way to reset the relationship between financial markets and the central bank. “The Fed needs clear market signals, as unfiltered as possible, from market internals,” Warsh said. Market participants, he added, should track real information across the economy and form their own expectations of output, employment and inflation.

Warsh also addressed the limits of economic forecasting, noting that with rapid changes in geopolitics, global supply chains and technology, “it's wise to be modest about what we can and cannot know.” He said the Fed will work to construct more reliable models and more robust rules to guide policy decisions, while acknowledging that “accuracy in economic forecasting is still just an aspiration.”

On inflation, Warsh was direct about the central bank’s accountability. “The responsibility for 65 months of sustained, elevated inflation sits squarely with the central bank,” he said. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.”

Warsh also touched briefly on artificial intelligence and its uncertain economic impact, saying the Fed will examine the matter through a task force on productivity and jobs. He stressed that the task force’s recommendations “will come later and have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture.”

article.title: IT Services Company Spending $45M on Mesa HQ
article.excerpt: ER2 received approval from the Mesa Planning & Zoning Board for a new headquarters near Falcon Field Airport, with plans to invest approximately $45 million in a 155,000-square-foot industrial building.
article.body_html:
The Mesa Planning & Zoning Board has approved ER2's application for a new headquarters at the corner of McDowell and Greenfield roads. The IT services and technology equipment recycling company plans to invest approximately $45 million and nearly double its Valley footprint by building a 155,000-square-foot industrial headquarters on vacant land near Falcon Field Airport.

ER2 is currently headquartered in Mesa at 730 E. Southern Ave., with a Phoenix office at 1710 E. Washington St. The company began operations at its Mesa facility in 2012 and opened its Phoenix location in 2019 after outgrowing the Mesa site. The new headquarters will consolidate the two Valley facilities into one larger building, with space to support 250 to 300 employees.

The build-to-suit development will include a 155,597-square-foot light industrial building, featuring a 132,544-square-foot first floor and a 23,043-square-foot second floor. Planned amenities include a fitness center, sauna, golf simulator, gaming coves, production studio, and covered parking. LGE Design Build is listed as the architect, and Hunter Engineering is the civil engineer.

Details on construction timelines and financing were not included in the available reporting.

article.title: $36M renovation of historic Eastern Parkway Library breaks ground
article.excerpt: Work has begun on a $36 million transformation of Crown Heights' historic Eastern Parkway Library, expanding public space by more than 50 percent while preserving its century-old architecture.
article.body_html:
Work has begun on the $36 million transformation of Crown Heights' historic Eastern Parkway Library. Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday announced the start of the project, which will expand public space at the century-old Brooklyn Public Library branch at 1044 Eastern Parkway by more than 50 percent while preserving its historic architecture. Led by the city's Department of Design and Construction, the project is expected to be completed in summer 2028.

Established in 1914, the original two-story library was designed by Raymond F. Almirall and built as part of a $5.2 million gift from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie to establish a comprehensive library system across New York City. The Classical Revival-style building features a limestone facade and long, arched windows, with double-height reading rooms and mezzanines overlooking the lower level.

Designed by Allied Works, the renovation will expand the library's public space by 12,250 square feet and add a 13,400-square-foot, three-story wing along Schenectady Avenue. A new glass facade will bring more natural light into the library and make the building fully ADA-compliant, with a new elevator and entrance ramp. The facility will feature dedicated reading and learning spaces, including a multipurpose room, a main reading room, a teen zone, two children's zones, a STEAM room, a community room, and a classroom in the building's restored fireplace room.

The renovation will also add modern, energy-efficient lighting and upgrade the library's plumbing, HVAC, and fire alarm systems. After the renovation, the library is expected to achieve LEED Silver certification. Artwork by local artist Oasa DuVerney will be displayed throughout the library through the Department of Cultural Affairs' Percent for Art Program.

During construction, library services will continue at a temporary location provided by the Settlement Housing Fund, with furniture donated by IKEA and additional support for interim services provided by Amazon. The temporary branch is expected to open this fall. The project is funded by the Office of the Mayor, the City Council, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, and the state Assembly.

article.title: SK Telecom creates SK Horizon in $2.2B data center spin-off deal
article.excerpt: SKT has spun off SK Broadband's data center assets to create SK Horizon, a new AI data center and submarine cable subsidiary backed by KKR and a domestic consortium.
article.body_html:
SK Telecom (SKT) is spinning off SK Broadband's data center assets to establish SK Horizon, a new subsidiary focused on AI data center (AIDC) infrastructure and submarine cable operations. The South Korean operator signed deals with global investment firm KKR and a consortium made up of IMM Investment and Stonebridge Capital for a combined investment of 3.08 trillion Korean won (US$2.24 billion) in the new company.

Once the transaction is complete, KKR and the IMM-Stonebridge consortium will hold 29% and 20% stakes in SK Horizon respectively, while SKT will retain management control as the largest shareholder with a 51% stake. SKT aims to complete the spin-off from SK Broadband by the first quarter of next year, pending regulatory approvals and an extraordinary shareholders meeting.

SK Horizon will assume operation of eight existing data centers located in Seocho, Ilsan, Bundang, Gasan, Centum, Yangju and Pangyo, as well as two new AIDCs under construction in Ulsan and Guro. These facilities will provide a total IT capacity of 318MW. The company will also pursue phased expansion of its submarine cable infrastructure, which SKT describes as vital for global AI businesses.

"This governance restructuring is a proactive measure aimed at strengthening expertise and enabling faster execution in the AIDC business," said Kim Seong-soo, newly appointed CEO of SK Horizon. Kim is also CEO of SK Broadband, which will now focus on its fixed-line, media and enterprise businesses.

The spin-off completes the governance restructuring required for SKT to accelerate its AIDC expansion. Last month, SKT established SK Hyper, a new $510 million subsidiary focused on building GW-scale AI data centers across South Korea, with the aim of reaching a total capacity of 15GW by 2035. Under the new structure, SKT will oversee the SK Group's AIDC business as a whole, while SK Horizon expands existing infrastructure and SK Hyper focuses on business development for new AIDC projects.

article.title: Harrison Street, Meridian Buy 431K-SF NoVA Office Portfolio
article.excerpt: A joint venture including Meridian Group, Harrison Street Asset Management and HLM Associates acquired the Stoneleigh and Newbrook campuses in Chantilly, Va., targeting national security, defense and intelligence tenants.
article.body_html:
Meridian Group and Harrison Street Asset Management have acquired a five-building office portfolio in Chantilly, Va., as part of a broader push to attract national security, defense and intelligence firms as tenants. The joint venture, which also includes HLM Associates, acquired the Stoneleigh and Newbrook campuses totaling 431,000 square feet in the Westfields submarket of Fairfax County.

The buyers said they plan additional capital investments to expand secure-facility capabilities and to modernize infrastructure across the portfolio. The companies did not disclose pricing. Bisnow reported the sale price at approximately $67 million, citing a source familiar with the deal. The five properties are at 4800 and 4840 Westfields Boulevard and 14150, 14151 and 14155 Newbrook Drive. An affiliate of the RMR Group sold the properties, records show.

The acquisition is the first for Meridian's platform around secure, mission-critical facilities, according to Gary Block, the Bethesda-based firm's chief investment officer. "Our goal is to become a landlord of choice for both traditional government contractors and the growing universe of nontraditional defense and technology companies in the markets we serve," Block said in a statement.

Harrison Street, which has approximately $109 billion in assets under management, said the strategy targets specialized properties benefiting from government-related demand and high barriers to entry. HLM also has expertise in the development and operation of facilities supporting classified government operations. Additional financial terms and tenant details were not disclosed.

article.title: Bonaventure Acquires Ownership Interest in Maryland Apartment Community
article.excerpt: Bonaventure has acquired an ownership interest in Crescent at Chevy Chase, a 111-home community in Chevy Chase, Maryland, from Landmark Realty, Inc.
article.body_html:
Bonaventure, an operator-led multifamily real estate investment firm with approximately $2.9 billion in assets under management, announced that it has acquired an ownership interest in Crescent at Chevy Chase, a 111-home community at 3929 Landmark Court in Chevy Chase, Maryland, from Landmark Realty, Inc., the Chevy Chase-based firm that developed the property.

The investment was made through Bonaventure Multifamily Income Trust (BMIT), a non-traded real estate investment trust sponsored by Bonaventure. Bonaventure has assumed asset management of the community, and Willow Bridge Property Company has been engaged as the property manager. Landmark Realty, which designed, developed and has operated Crescent since its delivery, remains a partner in the ownership group. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed.

Delivered in 2024, Crescent at Chevy Chase comprises 111 apartment homes averaging 846 square feet across studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom floor plans. The community was constructed to the National Green Building Standard Emerald specifications and sits directly adjacent to the future Connecticut Avenue station on the Maryland Purple Line, expected to open in late 2027.

"Crescent at Chevy Chase is a community we intend to own for a very long time," said Dwight Dunton, Chief Executive Officer of Bonaventure. Cushman & Wakefield and Greystone arranged financing for the transaction. Further financial details were not disclosed.

article.title: Colliers Facilitates $23.15M Sale of Coolidge Corner Collection Portfolio in Brookline
article.excerpt: Colliers announced the $23.15 million sale of the nine-building Coolidge Corner Collection in Brookline, Massachusetts, on behalf of Ramon Realty.
article.body_html:
Colliers announced the $23.15 million sale of the Coolidge Corner Collection in Brookline, Massachusetts. The sale was facilitated on behalf of Ramon Realty by a Colliers team including Managing Director of Investment Sales Frank Petz, Senior Vice President Tim McGeary, Vice President Brett Curtis, and Senior Financial Analyst Matt Lombardi.

The nine-building, mixed-use portfolio includes properties at 223 and 229-231 St. Paul Street, 26-28 Browne Street, 395-397 Harvard Street, 7 Naples Road, and 1343 Beacon Street. Totaling 65,262 square feet, the portfolio comprises 49 residential units and three commercial spaces and was acquired by City Realty.

The offering attracted strong interest from local, regional, and national investors despite uncertainty surrounding the proposed statewide rent-control ballot initiative. The portfolio offered a value-add opportunity alongside 96% occupancy, with only 12% of units fully renovated and 57% partially upgraded.

"The Coolidge Corner Collection represents the type of high-quality multifamily asset that will continue to attract investors," Frank Petz said. "The depth of interest we saw throughout the process, despite uncertainty surrounding the proposed rent-control ballot initiative, speaks to investors' conviction in Brookline and the opportunity for the portfolio to create additional value through continued unit improvements."

The sale follows the recent expansion of Colliers' multifamily platform in Boston with the additional hires of McGeary and Curtis in July. Colliers reported $5.7 billion in annual revenues, 24,000 professionals, and $109 billion in assets under management.

article.title: JLL Arranges $13.5M Sale and Financing of 96-Room Residence Inn in Danvers Massachusetts
article.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged the $13.5 million sale and financing of the 96-room Residence Inn Boston North Shore/Danvers, an extended-stay hotel with approved conversion rights to an 88-unit multifamily residential community.
article.body_html:
JLL Capital Markets announced it arranged the $13.5 million sale and financing of the 96-room Residence Inn Boston North Shore/Danvers, an extended-stay hotel with approved conversion rights to an 88-unit multifamily residential community. The property is located at 51 Newbury St. in Danvers, Massachusetts, approximately 20 miles north of Boston.

JLL represented the seller, an affiliate of PEG Companies, Inc., in the transaction. Torrington acquired the asset and plans to move forward with a multifamily conversion after an initial period of continued hotel operations under the Residence Inn brand. JLL also worked on behalf of Torrington to secure financing for the acquisition.

Built in 1989 on 4.11 acres, the property sits at the junction of Interstate 95, U.S. Route 1 and Route 128, providing direct access to downtown Boston, Logan International Airport and the North Shore region. Current ownership secured municipal zoning approvals for an 88-unit apartment conversion from the Danvers Zoning Board of Appeals.

"The North Shore continues to benefit from its position as a high-barrier suburban alternative to Boston, with strong fundamentals supporting both hospitality and residential demand," said Alan Suzuki, Senior Managing Director at JLL. "Torrington recognized the value in acquiring an income-producing hotel asset with a de-risked pathway to capitalize on severe housing supply constraints and robust rental demand in one of Greater Boston's most connected suburban markets."

Parts Town Unlimited Signs 538,450 SF Industrial Lease in Pendergrass, Georgia

article.title: Parts Town Unlimited Signs 538,450 SF Industrial Lease in Pendergrass, Georgia
article.excerpt: Parts Town Unlimited has signed a 538,450-square-foot, full-building lease at Jackson 85 North Business Park in Pendergrass, about 57 miles northeast of Atlanta via I-85.
article.body_html:
Parts Town Unlimited has signed a 538,450-square-foot, full-building lease at Jackson 85 North Business Park in Pendergrass, Georgia, about 57 miles northeast of Atlanta via I-85. The owner is a joint venture between affiliates Trammell Crow Co. (TCC) and CBRE Investment Management, which is acting as a landlord on behalf of a fund it manages.

Parts Town Unlimited is a global parent company and distributor of original equipment manufacturer replacement parts for the food service, residential appliance and HVAC industries. The firm will move into Building One by the end of the year. According to TCC, the facility will be the company's largest fulfillment center to date.

Phase I of Jackson 85 North features two speculative warehouse buildings totaling more than 1.5 million square feet across 215 acres. Both cross-dock warehouses include 40-foot clear heights, 185-foot concrete truck courts, more than 290 dock door positions, four drive-in ramps and a 3,900-square-foot air-conditioned office area. The buildings also feature a roofing system that can accommodate future solar panels, ample electrical service and an ESFR fire protection system.

Financial terms of the lease were not disclosed in the source report.

drafts.title: Kevin Warsh Notes Inflation Concerns But Offers No Clues as to Next Fed Decision

article.title: Kevin Warsh Notes Inflation Concerns But Offers No Clues as to Next Fed Decision
article.excerpt: The Fed chair said in Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not 'meaningfully improved.'
article.body_html:
New Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did not tip his hand Friday about whether an interest rate hike is on the horizon but did voice concerns about a continued trend of higher inflation. "I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision," Warsh said in prepared remarks at the central bank's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyo. "We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do."

Warsh, who assumed the Fed leadership post in June from Jerome Powell, stressed that the Federal Open Market Committee remains committed to keeping its 2 percent annual inflation rate as a target. He said that recent personal consumption expenditures and the consumer price index have performed "better than expected," but also noted that underlying inflation trends have not "meaningfully improved."

The FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rates at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent during Warsh's first two meetings. Warsh has sought to change the Fed's long-standing forward-guidance policy often used by markets when interpreting the central bank's data, a position he re-emphasized Friday. "We determine the path of short-term interest rates, and market participants will always try to anticipate what we will do next," Warsh said. "But we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade."

The FOMC's next meeting is scheduled for Sept. 15-16. Markets have priced in about a 50 percent chance of a rate hike based on Investing.com's latest Fed rate monitor tool.
